abstract:
<jats:p>A Gram-stain-positive, moderately halophilic, aerobic, endospore-forming, rod-shaped bacterium, designated strain DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>, was isolated from hypersaline sediment collected from the Dalangtan Playa in the Qaidam Basin, Northwest PR China. Growth occurred within 0–21.6% (w/v) NaCl (optimum 7.2%) at pH 5.5–9.0 (optimum pH 7.0) and at 4–45 °C (optimum 37 °C). Phylogeny based on 16S rRNA gene sequences indicated that strain DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> belonged to the genus <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="genus">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.13146" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic>, with high 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity to <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="species">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.13774" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus halophilus</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic> EN8d<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (99.5 %), <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="species">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.36319" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus terrae</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic> JSM 102062<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (99.4 %), <jats:italic>Virgibacillus senegalensis</jats:italic> SK-1<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (99.3 %) and <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="species">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.14471" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus albus</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic> NHBX5<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (98.3 %). The G+C content of the chromosomal DNA was 43.6 mol %. The average amino acid identity, average nucleotide identity and digital DNA–DNA hybridization values between strain DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> and the four close type strains were 71.2–93.3, 74.0–90.5 and 20.0–41.4 %, respectively. The whole genomic analysis showed that strain DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> constituted a different taxon separated from the recognized <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="genus">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.13146" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic> species. The major cellular fatty acids were anteiso-C<jats:sub>15 : 0</jats:sub>, anteiso-C<jats:sub>17 : 0</jats:sub>, iso-C<jats:sub>16 : 0</jats:sub>, C<jats:sub>16 : 0</jats:sub> and iso-C<jats:sub>15 : 0</jats:sub>. The type strain contained cell-wall peptidoglycan based on diaminopimelic acid and possessed menaquinone-7 as the major respiratory isoprenoid quinone. The polar lipid pattern consisted of diphosphatidylglycerol, phosphatidylglycerol, four unidentified glycolipids, phosphatidylcholine, aminophospholipid, aminolipid and seven unidentified phospholipids. The combined data from phenotypic and genotypic studies demonstrated that strain DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> represents a novel species of the genus <jats:italic>
                     <jats:named-content content-type="genus">
                        <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="uri" xlink:href="http://doi.org/10.1601/nm.13146" xlink:type="simple">Sediminibacillus</jats:ext-link>
                     </jats:named-content>
                  </jats:italic>, for which the name <jats:italic>Sediminibacillus dalangtanensis</jats:italic> sp. nov. is proposed, the type strain is DP4-553-S<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (=MCCC 1K03838<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>= KCTC 43250<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>).</jats:p>
title: Sediminibacillus dalangtanensis sp. nov., a moderate halophile isolated from hypersaline sediments of the Qaidam Basin in Northwest China

abstract: <jats:p>Halophytes hold significance for soil desalination and co-cultivation in farming systems. A major impediment to their use is the standardization of their performance, since halophytes are mainly wild plants, in addition to the need for a constant supply of the most suitable species. In this work, using highly salt-tolerant clones of Arthrocaulon macrostachyum obtained previously from in vitro micropropagation and selection, we compared the physiological and biochemical responses of these clones and their wild counterparts to high salinity levels (428 mM NaCl) under glasshouse conditions. In vitro-derived clones displayed a superior biomass production (27%) and higher chloride concentration in the shoot (28%), compared to the wild plants. On the other hand, wild specimens showed more stress symptoms and a less efficient photosynthesis, which was correlated with higher levels of oxidative stress and with a remarkable induction of peroxidase activity. Therefore, a higher incidence of salinity-related oxidative stress in the wild halophytes in comparison to the clones is concluded. This represents the first ex vitro evaluation of halophyte clones selected by means of micropropagation and provides insights into the salinity tolerance mechanisms of A. macrostachyum.</jats:p>
title: In Vitro-Selected Clones of the Halophyte Arthrocaulon macrostachyum Display Enhanced Salinity Stress Tolerance

abstract:
<jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>
<jats:list list-type="bullet">

<jats:list-item><jats:p>Halophytes tolerate high salinity levels that would kill conventional crops. Understanding salt tolerance mechanisms will provide clues for breeding salt‐tolerant plants. Many halophytes, such as quinoa (<jats:italic>Chenopodium quinoa</jats:italic>), are covered by a layer of epidermal bladder cells (EBCs) that are thought to mediate salt tolerance by serving as salt dumps.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>We isolated an <jats:italic>epidermal bladder cell‐free</jats:italic> (<jats:italic>ebcf</jats:italic>) quinoa mutant that completely lacked EBCs and was mutated in <jats:italic>REBC</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>REBC‐like1</jats:italic>. This mutant showed no loss of salt stress tolerance.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>When wild‐type quinoa plants were exposed to saline soil, EBCs accumulated potassium (K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>) as the major cation, in quantities far exceeding those of sodium (Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>). Emerging leaves densely packed with EBCs had the lowest Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> content, whereas old leaves with deflated EBCs served as Na<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> sinks. When the leaves expanded, K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup> was recycled from EBCs, resulting in turgor loss that led to a progressive deflation of EBCs.</jats:p></jats:list-item>

<jats:list-item><jats:p>Our findings suggest that EBCs in young leaves serve as a K<jats:sup>+</jats:sup>‐powered hydrodynamic system that functions as a water sink for solute storage. Sodium ions accumulate within old leaves that subsequently wilt and are shed. This mechanism improves the survival of quinoa under high salinity conditions.</jats:p></jats:list-item>
</jats:list>
</jats:p>
title: The epidermal bladder cell‐free mutant of the salt‐tolerant quinoa challenges our understanding of halophyte crop salinity tolerance

abstract: <jats:p>Understanding heavy metal behavior in arid saline soils is critical for phytoremediation in degraded lands. This study investigated metal distribution and plant enrichment in the Tarim Basin using 323 soil and 55 plant samples (Populus euphratica, Tamarix ramosissima, cotton, jujube). Analyses included redundancy analysis (RDA) and bioconcentration factor (BCF) assessments. Key findings reveal that elevated salinity (total salts, TS > 200 g/kg) and alkalinity (pH > 8.5) immobilized As, Cd, Cu, and Zn. Precipitation and competitive leaching reduced metal mobility by 42–68%. Plant enrichment strategies diverged significantly: P. euphratica hyperaccumulated Cd (BCF = 1.59) and Zn (BCF = 2.41), while T. ramosissima accumulated As and Pb (BCF > 0.05). Conversely, cotton posed Hg transfer risks (BCF = 2.15), and jujube approached Cd safety thresholds in phosphorus-rich soils. RDA indicated that pH and total salinity (TS) jointly suppressed metal bioavailability, explaining 57.6% of variance. Total phosphorus (TP) and soil organic carbon (SOC) enhanced metal availability (36.8% variance), with notable TP-Cd synergy (Pearson’s r = 0.42). We propose a dual-threshold management framework: (1) leveraging salinity–alkalinity suppression (TS > 200 g/kg + pH > 8.5) for natural immobilization; and (2) implementing TP control (TP > 0.8 g/kg) to mitigate crop Cd risks. P. euphratica demonstrates targeted phytoremediation potential for degraded saline agricultural systems. This framework guides practical management by spatially delineating zones for natural immobilization versus targeted remediation (e.g., P. euphratica planting in Cd/Zn hotspots) and implementing phosphorus control in high-risk croplands.</jats:p>
title: Halophyte-Mediated Metal Immobilization and Divergent Enrichment in Arid Degraded Soils: Mechanisms and Remediation Framework for the Tarim Basin, China

abstract: <jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>Actin‐depolymerizing factors (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>s) maintain the cellular actin network dynamics by regulating severing and disassembly of actin filaments in response to environmental cues. An <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content></jats:italic> isolated from a monocot halophyte, <jats:italic>Spartina alterniflora</jats:italic> (<jats:italic>Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic>), imparted significantly higher level of drought and salinity tolerance when expressed in rice than its rice homologue <jats:italic>Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic>. Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 differs from Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 by a few amino acid residues, including a substitution in the regulatory phosphorylation site serine‐6, which accounted for its weak interaction with Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">CDPK</jats:styled-content>6 (calcium‐dependent protein kinase), thus resulting in an increased efficacy of Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 and enhanced cellular actin dynamics. Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 overexpression preserved the actin filament organization better in rice protoplasts under desiccation stress. The predicted tertiary structure of Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 showed a longer F‐loop than Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 that could have contributed to higher actin‐binding affinity and rapid F‐actin depolymerization in vitro by Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2. Rice transgenics constitutively overexpressing <jats:italic>Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic> (<jats:italic>Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic>‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OE</jats:styled-content>) showed better growth, relative water content, and photosynthetic and agronomic yield under drought conditions than wild‐type (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WT</jats:styled-content>) and <jats:italic>Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic> overexpressers (<jats:italic>Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content></jats:italic>2‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OE</jats:styled-content>). <jats:italic>Sa<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic>‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OE</jats:styled-content> preserved intact grana structure after prolonged drought stress, whereas <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WT</jats:styled-content> and <jats:italic>Os<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2</jats:italic>‐<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">OE</jats:styled-content> presented highly damaged and disorganized grana stacking. The possible role of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 in transactivation was hypothesized from the comparative transcriptome analyses, which showed significant differential expression of stress‐related genes including interacting partners of <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content>2 in overexpressers. Identification of a complex, differential interactome decorating or regulating stress‐modulated cytoskeleton driven by <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">ADF</jats:styled-content> isoforms will lead us to key pathways that could be potential target for genome engineering to improve abiotic stress tolerance in agricultural crops.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>
            Halophytes are important coastal plants often used for the remediation of saline coastal soils.
            <jats:named-content content-type="genus-species">Limonium sinense</jats:named-content>
            is well known for its medical properties and phytoremediation of saline soils. However, excessive exploitation and utilization have made the wild resource endangered. The use of endophytic and rhizosphere bacteria may be one of the suitable ways to solve the problem. This study was undertaken to develop approaches to improve the growth of
            <jats:named-content content-type="genus-species">L. sinense</jats:named-content>
            using endophytes. The application of actinobacterial endophytes ameliorated salt stress damage of the host via complex physiological and molecular mechanisms. The results also highlight the potential of using habitat-adapted, symbiotic, indigenous endophytic bacteria to enhance the growth and ameliorate abiotic stress damage of host plants growing in special habitats.
          </jats:p>
title: Diversity of Bacterial Microbiota of Coastal Halophyte Limonium sinense and Amelioration of Salinity Stress Damage by Symbiotic Plant Growth-Promoting Actinobacterium Glutamicibacter halophytocola KLBMP 5180
